The energy stored in a stretched or compressed spring is **½kx²**.
**Step 1 — write the restoring force.** Hooke's law gives
F = kx
for an extension x, the force growing in **proportion** to the extension ✓
**Step 2 — integrate to find the work done.** Because the force changes as the spring
stretches, the work is an integral, not a simple product:
U = ∫₀ˣ kx' dx'
= k[x'²/2]₀ˣ
= **½kx²** ✓
**Step 3 — read it off the graph.** A plot of F against x is a straight line of slope k ✓
The work is the **area under it** - a triangle of base x and height kx:
area = ½(x)(kx) = **½kx²** ✓ the same result geometrically.
**Why the factor of ½ appears.** The force starts at **zero** and rises to kx, so the
**average** force over the stretch is kx/2 ✓ Multiplying that average by the distance x
gives ½kx². Using the final force kx throughout would wrongly give kx², which is the
second option.
**Why the energy is the same in compression.** x appears **squared**, so the sign of the
displacement does not matter ✓ A spring squeezed by 2 cm stores exactly as much as one
stretched by 2 cm.
**A worked value.** For k = 200 N m⁻¹ and x = 0·1 m:
U = ½(200)(0·01) = **1 J** ✓
and doubling the extension to 0·2 m gives **4 J** - four times as much, because of the
square.
**Where this energy goes.** Released, it converts entirely to kinetic energy ✓ which is
the basis of catapults, spring guns, clockwork and the oscillation of a mass on a spring.
**Reading the distractors.** **2kx²** ✗ is four times too large. **√2 kx²** ✗ matches no
integration. **None of these** ✗ is unnecessary, since ½kx² is offered ✓
∴ kx²/2.

A magnetic force is always **perpendicular to the velocity**, so it can never do work.
**Step 1 — write the magnetic force.**
F̄ = q(v̄ x B̄)
A cross product is perpendicular to both of its factors, so **F̄ ⟂ v̄** always ✓
**Step 2 — compute the power it delivers.**
P = F̄ · v̄
= q(v̄ x B̄) · v̄
= **0** ✓
since any vector dotted with a cross product containing itself vanishes.
**Step 3 — conclude.** Zero power means **zero work** at every instant, so a magnetic
force can change a particle's **direction** but never its **speed** ✓ It therefore makes
no contribution whatever to the kinetic energy, and may be left out of any energy
calculation - which is exactly what the question asks about.
**The familiar consequence.** A charged particle in a uniform magnetic field moves in a
**circle at constant speed** ✓ The field bends the path continuously but never speeds the
particle up - which is why a cyclotron needs a separate **electric** field to accelerate
its particles, with the magnetic field only to steer them.
**Why the other explanations fail.**
"**equal and opposite, so no net effect**" ✗ - the two forces act on **different**
particles, so they do not cancel in the way an action-reaction pair acting on one body
would. They certainly change each particle's path.
"**equal and opposite but non-zero work**" ✗ - each force does **exactly zero** work
individually, not merely equal and opposite amounts.
"**necessarily negligible**" ✗ - magnetic forces between moving charges can be
appreciable, and are not neglected in calculating the **motion**; they are omitted only
from the **energy** balance ✓
**The precise statement.** The magnetic force is not negligible and it is not cancelled;
it is **workless** ✓ That is a much stronger and more useful fact.
∴ the magnetic forces do not work on each particle.

Both particles feel the same **initial** force, but the lighter one accelerates away
faster and so covers more distance - and work is force times distance.
**Step 1 — compare the forces at the start.** A positron and a proton carry the **same
charge** +e, so at the same distance d from the fixed proton each feels the same
repulsive force ✓
**Step 2 — compare the masses.** A positron has the mass of an **electron**, about
**1/1836** of a proton's ✓
**Step 3 — compare the accelerations.** With a = F/m, the positron's initial
acceleration is **1836 times greater** ✓
**Step 4 — compare the distances travelled in the same time t.** The positron moves away
far more rapidly, so in the same interval it covers a **much larger distance** ✓
**Step 5 — compare the work done.** Work is the integral of F over the path travelled.
Over a longer path - starting from the same force - the positron has **more work done on
it** ✓
**Step 6 — check with energy directly.** The work done equals the drop in potential
energy over the distance covered:
W = kq²/d − kq²/r_final
The positron reaches a larger r_final, so its kq²/r_final is **smaller** and the
difference is **larger** ✓ The same conclusion, from the energy side.
**Why the force weakening does not reverse this.** It is true that the force on the
positron falls off faster, because it recedes faster ✓ But it recedes so much further
that the **total** work still exceeds the proton's - the integral is dominated by the
extra distance, not reduced by the weaker tail.
**A limiting check.** As t → ∞ the positron has gained the full available energy kq²/d,
while the heavy proton is still lumbering outward with only part of it ✓ At every finite
time the positron is ahead.
**Reading the distractors.** "**Same, as the same force law is involved**" ✗ confuses
equal **forces** with equal **work** - work also needs distance. "**Less for the
positron**" ✗ reverses the conclusion. "**Same as the work done on the stationary
proton**" ✗ - the fixed proton does not move, so **no** work is done on it ✓
∴ more for the case of a positron, as the positron moves away a larger distance.

Standing up requires an **upward acceleration** at first and none at the end, so the
reaction force cannot be constant.
**Step 1 — apply Newton's second law vertically.** With N the ground's reaction and the
man's centre of mass accelerating upward at a:
N − mg = ma
**N = m(g + a)** ✓
**Step 2 — follow the motion in stages.**
**starting to rise**: the centre of mass accelerates **upward**, so a > 0 and
**N > mg** ✓
**midway**: moving up steadily, a ≈ 0 and N ≈ mg
**slowing to a stop**: the upward motion must be halted, so a < 0 and **N < mg**
**fully upright and still**: a = 0 and **N = mg** ✓
**Step 3 — match to the options.** The reaction is **at first greater than mg, and later
becomes equal to mg** ✓ - the description that captures both the push at the start and
the settled state at the end.
**Why it cannot be constant at mg.** If N were always mg, the net force would always be
zero and the man's centre of mass, starting at rest, would **never move** ✓ Standing up
is impossible without at some point pushing harder than one's weight.
**Why it cannot always be greater than mg.** Once the man is standing still, the
acceleration is zero and the reaction is **exactly mg** ✓ The force must come back down.
**A rough numerical picture.** A 60 kg man raising his centre of mass 0·4 m in about
1 second has an average upward acceleration of roughly 1·6 m s⁻² over the first half:
N ≈ 60(9·8 + 1·6) = **684 N** against a weight of **588 N** ✓ about 16% more, which is
about what a bathroom scale registers if one stands up on it.
**The everyday confirmation.** Stand on a weighing scale and rise quickly from a squat:
the needle **flicks up** first, then dips below, then settles at your weight ✓ exactly
the sequence the equation predicts.
∴ at first greater than mg, and later becomes equal to mg.

In free fall under gravity alone, kinetic and potential energy are exchanged but their
**sum** does not change.
**Step 1 — track the kinetic energy.** The body speeds up as it falls, so
**KE increases** ✗ not constant.
**Step 2 — track the potential energy.** Its height falls, so
**PE decreases** ✗ not constant.
**Step 3 — track the total.** Gravity is a **conservative** force, and in a vacuum there
is no air resistance to dissipate anything ✓ So
**KE + PE = constant** ✓
Every joule the potential energy loses, the kinetic energy gains.
**Step 4 — track the momentum.** p = mv, and v grows steadily during the fall, so
**momentum increases** ✗ Gravity is an external force acting on the body, so its
momentum is not conserved - only the momentum of the body-plus-Earth system would be.
**A worked check.** A 2 kg body dropped from 20 m, with g = 10 m s⁻²:
at the top: PE = 2(10)(20) = **400 J**, KE = **0**, total **400 J**
at 10 m: v² = 2(10)(10) = 200, so KE = ½(2)(200) = **200 J**, PE = **200 J**, total
**400 J** ✓
at the ground: KE = **400 J**, PE = **0**, total **400 J** ✓
unchanged throughout, while every other quantity has altered.
**Why "in vacuum" is stated.** Air resistance is **non-conservative** ✓ With it, some
mechanical energy becomes heat and the total steadily falls - a body reaching terminal
velocity has constant KE but a continuously decreasing total. The vacuum is what makes
the conservation exact.
**The general principle.** When only conservative forces act, the total mechanical
energy is **conserved** ✓ This is the single most useful shortcut in mechanics: it
relates speeds and heights without ever mentioning time or acceleration.
**Reading the distractors.** **Kinetic energy** ✗ grows, **potential energy** ✗ falls,
and **momentum** ✗ grows - each changes, and only the total of the first two stays
fixed ✓
∴ total mechanical energy.
